The maximum adult body mass attained by the Spotted green goby Acentrogobius viridipunctatus reaches approximately 59.5 grams [Wwi = approximately 59.5 grams], an asymptotic value derived from length-weight relationships for the species. Field surveys indicate that individuals achieve a maximum total length of 16.5 centimeters [Li = 16.5 centimeters], which corresponds to the upper limit of their size range in estuarine habitats across Southeast Asia. In contrast, the onset of reproductive activity occurs at a considerably smaller body size, with individuals becoming capable of breeding once they attain a total length of 9 centimeters [Lp = 9 centimeters] and a corresponding body mass of approximately 9 grams [Wwp = approximately 9 grams]. This size threshold is consistent with the minimum pubertal dimensions observed in many small-bodied gobiids inhabiting tropical soft-bottom environments. Length-at-maturity data from trawl surveys in the Gulf of Thailand corroborate this pattern, suggesting that the species prioritizes rapid early growth to reach the reproductive window within its first year of life under favorable thermal regimes.

Embryonic development in Acentrogobius viridipunctatus proceeds rapidly at the water temperatures typical of its shallow coastal spawning grounds. Eggs incubated at 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C] complete their development and hatch after approximately 16 days [ab = approximately 16 days], a duration that aligns well with the incubation periods reported for the congener Acentrogobius pflaumii under comparable thermal conditions. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva is minute, with a wet weight at birth of only 0.0023 grams [Wwb = 0.0023 grams], reflecting the small egg diameter of roughly 0.48 millimeters characteristic of this species. This modest initial mass underscores the highly altricial state of the prolarvae at the moment of chorion rupture, requiring rapid yolk absorption and a swift transition to exogenous feeding within the planktonic environment. The elevated temperature of 28.2 °C appears to accelerate the cleavage and gastrulation stages, thereby shortening the overall pre-hatching period relative to populations experiencing cooler thermal regimes in higher-latitude portions of the genus range.

In spawning adults of the Spotted green goby, the gonadosomatic index (GSI) averaged 5% [GSI = 5%], measured under laboratory conditions at a stable temperature of 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C]. This relatively modest value suggests that females allocate a moderate fraction of their body reserves toward egg production at each spawning event, a pattern consistent with an iteroparous life-history strategy in which reproductive effort is distributed across multiple batches over the breeding season. The measurement was obtained from gravid females collected during the peak spawning period in the Gulf of Thailand, providing a robust empirical baseline for this key reproductive metric.

Longevity records for Acentrogobius viridipunctatus, compiled from mark-recapture studies conducted in mangrove-fringed estuaries at 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C], indicate that the species has a maximum lifespan of approximately 4.5 years [am = approximately 4.5 years]. This relatively extended lifespan, equivalent to roughly 1,642 days, is somewhat unusual for a small-bodied goby and may reflect the stable, resource-rich conditions of its preferred brackish-water habitats. In comparison, many tropical gobiids of similar adult size rarely survive beyond two or three years in the wild, suggesting that Acentrogobius viridipunctatus benefits from relatively low extrinsic mortality rates in its mangrove nursery grounds. The oldest individuals were recaptured in a protected estuarine reserve where fishing pressure is minimal, supporting the interpretation that the species can achieve its physiological longevity ceiling when anthropogenic disturbance is limited. This lifespan value provides an essential parameter for understanding the species' population turnover and its capacity to buffer against environmental stochasticity over multiple breeding seasons.

The combination of small neonatal mass, rapid juvenile growth, and a moderate reproductive lifespan defines the demographic profile of Acentrogobius viridipunctatus. Young-of-year individuals, having emerged from eggs with a birth mass of only 0.0023 grams [Wwb = 0.0023 grams] after a 16-day incubation (16 days) [ab = 16 days] at 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C], must undergo a dramatic increase in size to reach the 9-centimeter [Lp = 9-centimeter] length at puberty within their first year. The corresponding wet weight at puberty of 9 grams [Wwp = 9 grams] represents a more than three-thousand-fold increase from the larval mass at hatching, highlighting the intense growth demands placed upon these fish during the early juvenile phase. Once adulthood is attained, the maximum recorded adult mass of 59.5 grams [Wwi = 59.5 grams] provides an upper boundary on reproductive potential, as fecundity scales positively with body size in this species. The gonadosomatic index of 5% [GSI = 5%] measured at 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C] indicates that ovarian tissue accounted for about five percent of body mass in spawning females. These measurements were obtained in a species with a maximum lifespan of 4.5 years [am = 4.5 years] at a temperature of 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C].
